svg.font-family: Inter, Segoe UI, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
svg.title: Figure 1. Six ways traffic escapes, sorted by what decides the route
svg.desc: A table of six leak types organised by the mechanism that sends traffic outside the tunnel rather than by name. Name resolution reaching the wrong resolver is decided by the operating system's resolver order. Browser encrypted name resolution is decided by the browser, which overrides the tunnel's resolver. Real time communication address discovery is decided by the browser's own network stack. Traffic over the newer address family is decided by whether the tunnel carries it. Route injection from the local network is decided by the routing table, which an attacker can change. Kill switch failure is decided by the client software. The final column pairs each with the test that detects it, and the table notes that route injection leaves the tunnel connected and does not trigger a kill switch.
svg.text: Figure 1: Six Ways Traffic Escapes, and What Decides the Route
Leaks are usually taught as a list of names. Sorting them by which component chooses the path tells you where to look and what to fix.
Name lookups to the wrong resolver
The browser doing its own lookups
on by default, and rarely mentioned
The browser, which overrides the tunnel
A resolver test, but read it carefully
Traffic over the newer address family
now more than half of all traffic
Whether the tunnel carries it at all
Routes injected by the local network
The routing table, which somebody else set
The tunnel drops and traffic continues
Killing the process, not clicking disconnect
Four things this table makes visible that a list of names does not

g.text: Five of the six leave the tunnel connected. The client reports everything is fine, because from its point of view everything is. Only one is a connection failure.
Row five is invisible to every other row's test. The traffic never enters the tunnel, so there is nothing for the client to notice, and the guard has nothing to react to.
The last column is not one website. A single all-in-one page checks three of these and cannot see the other three, which is why the routine in Section 7 is longer than one link.
And row two is on by default in most browsers, so it is not a misconfiguration you made. It is a design decision somebody else made about your traffic.

svg.text: Test for the mechanism rather than the symptom. Two leaks that both show a wrong address need completely different fixes.
And a green result on an all-in-one page means three of these six were not tested at all.
